posts.author: Joe Farina
posts.content_md:
As I recall, someone used a water-absorbing material, and I think it was silica gel, and placed this into an alcohol/water mixture to soak up the water only, leaving relatively pure IPA.

Seems like a fair amount of trouble to go through, plus I think filtration of the final product would be essential, because we wouldn't want any particulate contamination in the final alcohol bath, as it could wreak havoc on the emulsion.

The 99% IPA can be a pain to get a hold of. A long time ago, John suggested the IPA from Abra Electronics (I think a link is on his website). That's what I use, and it comes by the gallon. The only problem is that they charge pretty heavily for shipping. The 99% IPA is also available from Techspray, in rather covenient pint-size containers, and I've used that also. The IPA itself is not really that expensive, but shipping usually adds significantly to the cost, so it would be ideal if you could find a local source and avoid shipping charges (something I have not been able to do). Dave said he gets his IPA by ordering it through a local pharmacy, but I haven't tried that.

posts.author: Colin Kaminski
posts.content_md: The only way I know of is to run the IPA through a still. An easy still would be to take a flask of diluted IPA and put it into dry ice. Skim off the ice and you should be close to 100%.

posts.author: Colin Kaminski
posts.content_md:
> **Dutchelm05:** Ahhh that is very clever, thanks ColinCan you explain how the still works? Do you heat the IPA and the evaporated stuff us pure IPA?

There are three ways I have distilled. One is to take advantage of the different boiling points of different liquids. One is to take advantage of different freezing points of different liquids. The third takes advantage of the different vapor pressures of different liquids.

In the freezing method you simply need to get it cold enough to freeze the water. I know for beer that happens at about 28F. If you remove the ice then you are "Jacking" the alcohol. I should mention that for beverage manufactures all three methods require a distillers license.

If you try the salt idea let me know how it works.

posts.author: Tom B.
posts.content_md:
The problem with distilling IPA/water is that the two liquids form an azeotrope (the combination has a lower boiling point than either) so it

is not possible to get pure IPA from distillation. The ratio you end up with is 12.6% water, 87.3% IPA. For ethanol/water it is better: 4% water, 96% ethanol.

See [http://www.solvent--recycling.com/azeotrope_1.html](http://www.solvent--recycling.com/azeotrope_1.html)

posts.author: Colin Kaminski
posts.content_md: Thank you for that, I was under the assumption that the only problem was the hygroscopic nature of alcohols.
